## ON THE FRONTISPIECE.

The Patriarch ABRAHAM, who, grave of countenance,
Stands upon the *Head* of the *Cornerstone* <note>A common Christian metaphor referring to Christ as the foundation of faith</note>, like an *Oak* of Mamre <note>The Oak of Mamre was the site where Abraham built an altar and received divine visitors</note>,
Whose *Weapon* served to loose Lot from Elam’s bonds <note>A reference to Genesis 14, where Abraham rescued his nephew Lot from the King of Elam</note>,
Just as his *Shepherd's Staff* watched over the cattle,
Faithfully embraces the true SAVING FAITH <note>original: "Heilgeloof"</note>:
Her *Sacrifice* makes him deaf to the flattery of passions;
While INCONSTANCY, whose unbound *Clothing*
Signifies fickle senses, like the *Globe* and *Feathers* <note>In 17th-century art, feathers and globes often symbolized instability and the fleeting nature of worldly things</note>;
IDOLATRY, who keeps her eye upon her *Household God*,
And SELF-LOVE, who gazes at her *False Jewelry*:
All these see themselves bridled by their Victor,
While OBEDIENCE, through her wings,
Makes his feet willing to undergo the *Yoke* of morals,
And swiftly strike the path of that *Law*, *Bridled*.
Thus he sees himself met by a Ray from Heaven,
And his *Possessions* and *Cattle* blessed upon Hebron’s mountains.

J. W.

# PREFACE.

I undertake to bring before the eyes of the modest Reader the most glorious example of Virtue and Piety found in either divine or human writings: **ABRAHAM THE PATRIARCH**; surely the most blessed and illustrious Personage (excepting, with all reverence, the Savior of the world, the Lord Jesus Christ) that the ages have ever seen. For who—to recall only sacred examples, for neither the Alexanders nor the Caesars <note>The author refers to Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar, the typical subjects of classical Greek and Roman epics, to argue that his biblical subject is more worthy of study than these secular "conquerors."</note> may be weighed here—who then, I say, of the divine Heroes of Faith obtained from the holy Writers so much renown for his untainted virtue or his pious and righteous conduct? Neither the divine Moses, the patient Job <note>original: "Hiob"</note>, the pious David, nor the wise Solomon obtained so many glorious names of praise and titles of honor. Upon whom do so many salutary promises rest? Whose name is, according to one of those very promises, so greatly glorified across the whole earth? A Name, which during his life [was] not

One might say: in this matter, I believe I have taken every possible care; however, against a lack of understanding, one cannot arm oneself:

->According to the capacity of the reader, books have their destiny. <note>original: "Pro captu lectoris habent sua fata libelli." This famous line from the Roman grammarian Terentianus Maurus suggests that a book's success or meaning depends on the reader's own perception.</note><-

But: because we humans, with our finite intellect, can only understand things piecemeal through reasoning <term>Redenkavelinge: the process of logical deduction or breaking down complex ideas into smaller parts to understand them</term> and composition; it has pleased the merciful Godhead <term>Godtheit: the divine essence or being of God</term> Himself to come to the aid of our weak understanding. He presents His infinite, incomprehensible Being—in which, in truth, no composition or division exists—from various perspectives, as if through so many aids to our contemplation. He even presents these specific views in His written Word using physical imagery and symbols <term>Zinnebeelden: allegorical representations or "sense-images" used to explain spiritual truths through physical objects</term> of human limbs, and even human passions. Thus, His sovereign and unchangeable Will is shown through the lens of a princely Council <term>Vorstelyken Raat: a metaphor for God's deliberative process, depicted as a royal court or assembly of divine advisors</term>, including counsels, thoughts, intentions, decrees, and the ways of God. Proofs of this are found everywhere in the holy pages, and especially—which we must not overlook—in the poetic portion <note>The "poetic portion" refers to books of the Bible such as Job, Psalms, and the Prophets, which use heavy metaphor and personification.</note> of the same, ready at hand.

One more word to the discerning and poetic Reader, and with that we take our leave; we request him to use our labor with as much benefit and edification as possible, and to that end to lay aside that nagging prejudice <term>vooroordeel</term> by which one immediately rejects everything that is new, as soon as one finds it not precisely consistent with this or that arbitrary law, put forward by foreigners <note>This likely refers to the strict rules of French Neoclassicism, which many Dutch poets of the time felt were too restrictive for religious epics.</note>,

<meta>This page continues the author’s preface, specifically concluding a defense against the rigid imposition of foreign (likely French Neoclassical) rules on Dutch poetry. It transitions from a critique of restrictive "laws" to a justification for the naturalistic and varied tone of the work.</meta>

# P R E F A C E.

*...scribed, and placed our free Art as a burdensome yoke upon the neck. I have not wished to bend the truth to foreign laws, or to manipulate it to my own hand, as a Painter does his Lay-figure <term>Leeman: a jointed wooden mannequin used by artists to study poses and proportions</term>; but I have preserved the same in its natural state, and left my History <note>In this context, "History" refers to the narrative or epic poem itself.</note>, into which we enter almost in the middle <note>A reference to the classical technique of "in media res," where a story begins in the midst of the action.</note>, to its own course. If my thoughts are sometimes found lowly, let one consider that my Hero is a Shepherd, and that the tone must also rise and fall according to the demands of the subject matter: but where the power of my spirit or art falters, let one take it for the best, and consider that a good tree produces leaves as well as flowers and fruits, under which the same hang safely, as if in a lovely shade, and ripen most fragrantly.*

Soon she rises, singing, from the earth;

While the previous page focused on the Muse's ascent, this poem compares Hoogvliet’s Christian subject matter to the classical epics of antiquity, specifically Virgil’s Aeneid.</meta>

->ON THE NEW PRINTING<-

->O F<-

# A B R A H A M,
## THE PATRIARCH,
->B Y<-
## ARNOLD HOOGVLIET.

Whoever takes delight in the sublime song of Poetry,
Whose soul could be enraptured by Maro’s <note>original: "Maroos" — Referring to the Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro, better known as Virgil, the author of the *Aeneid*.</note> heroic work,
See great ABRAHAM, as the Sun of all Heroes,
Dawning with new luster along HOOGVLIET’S literary meadow.

This Christian Hero of Song—who won the laurel crown
Neither through wild gusts of rhyming,
Nor by brain-disturbing water from Aganippe’s spring <term>Aganippe|In Greek mythology, a spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses, said to inspire those who drank from it. The poet here contrasts pagan inspiration with Christian grace.</term>,
But through God’s Pentecostal fire—
May wear such a wreath of honor to the glory of Heaven.

O Poets, who honor only the art of mythology <note>original: "Fabeldichtkunst" — literally "the art of fable-poetry," referring to classical Greek and Roman myths which were seen as "fables" compared to Biblical truth.</note>,
And inappropriately still decorate your work with its floral ornaments,
Learn here, along a nobler path, to strive directly toward the stars.

Let VIRGIL live, with his Hero <note>A reference to Aeneas, the protagonist of Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note>, immortalized on this earth;
But you, O HOOGVLIET! You, worthy of an even higher artistic reward,
Shall live, with your ABRAHAM, even in Heaven!

->*WILLEM VANDER POT.*<-

<summary>A dedicatory sonnet by Willem vander Pot praising Arnold Hoogvliet's epic poem. The author argues that Hoogvliet’s Christian subject matter and divine inspiration make his work superior to the classical pagan epics of Virgil.</summary>
<keywords>Arnold Hoogvliet, Willem vander Pot, Abraham the Patriarch, Virgil, Aganippe, Christian poetry, epic poetry, Pentecostal fire</keywords>

->ON THE FOURTH EDITION<-

->O F<-

# A B R A H A M,
### *THE PATRIARCH,*

->B Y<-

## ARNOLD HOOGVLIET.

The Heavenly Impulse, which sets the Spirit of Poetry <note>original: "Dichtgeest" — the personified genius or inspiration of the poet.</note> in motion,
Wishing once to show a proof of her powers,
Descended into the laurelled head of HOOGVLIET; she spurs on thoughts,
Conceptions, soul, and sense, with double zeal:

His Spirit of Poetry, thus ignited, rises above sun and moon,
Into the Palace of Heaven, on Cherubic wings <term>Cherubynenschachten|Literally "Cherub-shafts," referring to the wings of the Cherubim, the celestial beings who guard the presence of God.</term>;
Learns Angelic tones; sings of the Father of the generations,
The great ABRAHAM, and his sublime deeds.

Piety <note>original: "De Godsvrucht" — here personified as a figure who welcomes the poem into her temple.</note> had no sooner received this masterpiece
Than she placed it in the middle of her spacious Temple Hall.
Everyone hung upon the divine work with double attention.

O Poet-friend, ARNOLD, who for the fourth time,
Gifts your work to the world, your reward lies not in songs of praise!
Your Hero <note>Referring to the biblical Abraham, the subject of the epic.</note> awaits you with an eternal festive welcome!

->NIKOLAES VERSTEEG.<-

# ABRAHAM,
### THE
## PATRIARCH.
### THE FIRST BOOK.
### *C O N T E N T S.*

> The Patriarch Abram, driven by the pressure of famine,
> Comes to graze his hungry flock in Egyptian pastures;
> There Pharaoh's princes, enchanted by the beautiful face
> Of chaste Sarah, flatter the ear of their King,
> Who, thus ignited with love, snatches her from her sleeping-tent,
> And leads her to the palace in Memphis <note>An ancient capital of Egypt</note> among courtly women.
> He gathers the Council and makes a firm resolution
> To marry the Shepherdess after the festival of Isis <note>The Egyptian goddess of nature and magic</note>;
> While Abram, awaiting help from Heaven,
> Is presented with gifts, and already regarded as Pharaoh’s brother.

---

<margin>The poet’s purpose and Introduction.</margin>
It pleased me in days past to sing in Dutch <note>original: "Nederduitsche"; historically referring to the Low German or Dutch language</note> verses,
Of the Roman gods, and the history of their feasts and years,
Following in the tracks of Sulmo’s literary hero <note>A reference to the Roman poet Ovid, who was born in Sulmo and wrote the *Fasti*, a poem about the Roman calendar and festivals</note>;
But now, now I paint (as my own poetic vein <note>original: "zangaâr," literally "song-vein"</note> swells
With nobler passions, driven by a heavenly fire)
The great Father of the nations <note>Abraham</note> true to life:

# ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.
<meta>catchword: Depart,</meta>

Yes, it delights me to follow Abram on his journey to Canaan,
And to Egypt, and wherever that divine man
Wanders at the high Command, following him with my strings; <note>The poet refers to his "strings," meaning his lyre or the musical nature of his poetry.</note>
To reveal his wondrous communion with the Godhead;
And, in contemplation of his faith, hope,
And pure godliness, to soar through the whole course of his life
Until he, through God’s eternal grace,
Beholding the great Prince of Peace <note>A traditional Christian interpretation that Abraham "saw" the coming of Christ (the Prince of Peace) through his future descendants.</note> in his lineage,
Descends to the dark grave in his old age.

<margin>Address to the Theological Writers.</margin>
Come now, pious host of holy writers, come
Strengthen my weak spirit in this noble undertaking,
Learned men, teach me to write Biblical truth!
O industrious bees, who, from your youth onwards,
Have wandered through the botanical gardens of the sacred pages
To seek out the honey;
Forgive me if my spirit, wandering through the books,
Should greedily feed upon your delicacies,
That precious stock for my Biblical poetry:
If I draw honey from your full honeycombs;
Forgive me, I shall leave it there again for your benefit:
And perhaps that sweetness, with new fragrance and style,
Will lure you back to the field of my paper.

<margin>He sets unbelief aside.</margin>
But you, the Lost, you, O wanton minds,
O sharp wits, who dare to assault God’s truth,
And mock holy poetry, as if its subject were too lowly,
And its scriptural food <note>original: "letterspys," literally "letter-food," referring to the substance of the written Word.</note> too bland for your strong stomachs;

He invokes the "holy writers" (theologians and scholars) for inspiration, comparing their scholarly work to honey that he hopes to refine into poetry, while rebuking those who mock religious literature.</summary>

# THE FIRST BOOK.
<meta>catchword: Give</meta>

Depart, depart to the side, before you might hinder my beginning;
I do not sing for you: I sing only for Abraham's children. <note>The author distinguishes his audience; he is not writing for skeptics or the "unbelieving," but for the faithful who consider themselves spiritual descendants of Abraham.</note>
I scatter my roses for the spiritual Seed
Of the great Father, who, with a reverent face,
Bows his humble soul, like full ears of grain,
Before the truth of the divine pages,
While slander rages, and blusters, glowing with wrath,
And grows like sterile grain on steeper stalks.
<margin>He calls upon the Godhead for assistance.</margin>
O Heavenly Monarch! whose eyes never sleep,
Who through your omnipotence created the great Universe!
Infinite Being! who, in the highest vault,
Has the most perfect object of your love in yourself,
And yet casts your eye upon man, and his works!
O Father of mercy! ah, please strengthen my spirit,
As I set your holy promise and wondrous dealings with
Your heart-friend <term>Abraham</term><note>Abraham is traditionally referred to as the "Friend of God" (Khalil Allah in Arabic tradition, and similarly in Judeo-Christian texts), signifying a unique intimacy with the Divine.</note> to biblical tones!
Ah! let a spark of the divine fire of love,
That pained You with compassion for man's salvation,
Inflame my soul with a pure heavenly glow!
Ah! let a single ray enlighten my mind;
A ray of wisdom, shot from the <term>Sun of Salvation</term>;<note>original: "Heilzon." A metaphorical reference to God or Christ as the source of spiritual light and healing.</note>
A light of truth, sprung from your sanctuary;
A radiance of soul-peace, from your all-sufficiency:
So that your splendor may be spread in my poem!
Lead me, O Sun of Salvation! on dark letter-paths! <note>The "dark letter-paths" refer to the difficult or obscure passages of ancient scripture that the poet must navigate.</note>
O Spirit! guide my spirit on the track of the holy pages!

# ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.
<meta>catchword: It seemed</meta>

My Lord remembers (thus began that <term>Rose-mouth</term><note>original: "Rozemont." A conventional poetic epithet in 17th-century Dutch literature, meaning "Rose-mouth," used here to emphasize Sarah’s beauty despite her age.</note>)
How you, before we stepped onto Egypt’s fertile ground,
To dwell here for a time as strangers;
Revealed your fear to me, and the anxieties of your soul
For this beauty, which Heaven still preserves,
A gift of nature, but of a worrisome nature:
How you commanded that I should call myself your **Sister**;
So that they might not kill you because of me, and that we might
Live together more peacefully among this strange and wanton people.
This lies heavy on my heart: it seems to me I see a cloud
Of adversities, which I surely have to expect.
<margin>Concerning Abram's command that she should call herself his Sister.</margin>
I labor under mountains of anxious thoughts,
Sleep flees my eyes; or when it creeps upon me,
And now and then steals into my tired limbs,
Then I startle and awake from grim and fearful dreams.
Not that I shrink from following your commands,
My **Abram**, no, oh no; the sorrows I endure
Arise from the fear that you might die because of me.
Could this outward beauty still bring forth such great misfortune,
In my old age of sixty-five years?
May the <term>Most High</term><note>original: "d'Opperste." A reference to God.</note>, who appeared to you before, prevent that!
But this wondrous dream alone burdens my heart:
I dreamed that I, in the midst of the valleys,
Saw a beautiful rose parade in its full splendor:
It stood on display throughout the summer heat,
And remained, in scent and color and luster, just as beautiful.

# THE FIRST BOOK.
<meta>catchword: My</meta>

It seemed as if Heaven, through a wondrous power,
Preserved that flower, so pleasant in everyone’s eyes,
From the autumn storms. It seemed to me I saw
How that rose lay quite tenderly and close to your heart;
But, when you thought to care for this flower the most,
You found it, alas! on an early morning,
Stolen from the garden, and snatched from its place.
I awoke, and this dream remains pressed upon my soul.
Here Lady **Sara** fell silent, and a deep sigh, flown
From her bosom, forced a stream of tears from her eyes,
Which flowed from her cheeks onto her white breast:
Just as the morning dew sprays the leaves wet,
While a breeze comes creeping into the flower garden,
And makes those pearls drip onto the rosebuds.
<margin>
*She is comforted, and put at ease.*
</margin>
The <term>pious Father</term><note>original: "vrome Vader." A traditional honorific for the patriarch Abraham.</note>, himself moved by this state,
Dries her tears, and presses her tender hand;
He comforts his spouse thus: take courage, my **Chosen One**,
I hope your dream will be but a dream—that is, vanity.
But if misfortune wills that the <term>wanton people</term><note>original: "dartle lantaart." This is likely an OCR error for "landaart" (people of the land/nation), referring to the Egyptians whom Abraham fears will be overcome by lust.</note> lurk
For your beauty, driven by a hot passion;
He <note>Referring to the ruler of the land.</note> will attempt to buy you through service,
Where otherwise violence might dissolve the <term>marriage bond</term><note>original: "huwlyksbant." Abraham fears that if he is known as her husband, the Egyptians will kill him to "legally" take her; by posing as her brother, he hopes to negotiate and delay.</note>.
My tender care for you has devised this invention:
If you are desired for marriage, you remain yet in my power.
One shall constantly stretch the wedding day longer,
Until we finally depart again from this place.

### ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.
<meta>catchword: In</meta>

"My **Beautiful One**, be at ease; the all-seeing Godhead lives,
Who has guided us thus far, and has bountifully blessed us.
Let us cast our cares upon God’s omnipotence:
He shall send His light and clarity into the darkness,
And show, after this sorrow, His <term>saving countenance</term><note>original: "heilryk aangezicht." A poetic way of describing God’s favor and divine presence.</note>."

<margin>Rumor spreads through Memphis of the arrival of a strange multitude of people.</margin>
The sun had three times, with a joyful and smiling countenance,
Clad in shining gold, risen in the east,
And had now three times, weary from her day's journey,
Extinguished her torch in the <term>sea of Libya</term><note>original: "zee van Libië." In the geography of this period, the Mediterranean or the waters to the west of Egypt were often referred to as the Libyan sea; here it signifies the sunset.</note>;
When swift **Rumor**, which, fertile in the spreading
Of new tidings, flew along the streets and meadows of **Memphis**,
Called out from a hundred mouths how, near the city,
A strange multitude had struck camp.
The country folk were questioned as they came to market with their wares.
One said: "It is native people; they are Egyptians
From **Coptos**<note>original: "Koptos." An ancient city on the Nile that served as a major trading hub for goods coming from the Red Sea.</note>, accustomed to coming here with their grain."
Another: "They are **Arabs** with camels, heavily laden
With cloves, cinnamon, and the scent of incense for offerings,
And balsam perfumes for the hair of courtly ladies."
Yet another mingles something else into the mix.
Thus lies run, through the ignorant and wild commoners,
Constantly ahead of the truth, with unequal strides:
Just as an unbridled horse prances with swift limbs,
And runs and neighs, until it stops before a ditch,
And, exhausted, awaits its embarrassed master.

->### ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.<-
<meta>catchword: While</meta>

<margin>He desires to have Sarah at the court.</margin>
At last Pharaoh says: "I desire that they go once more
To Goshen, and fetch the beautiful Sarah here:
I feel a wondrous desire to behold that fresh countenance:
Lead her into the palace among the court's <term>ladies-in-waiting</term><note>original: "staatjonkvrouwen." Noblewomen who serve at a royal court.</note>."
He takes a golden cup full of <term>Meroitic wine</term><note>original: "Meroëëfchen wyn." Wine from Meroë, an ancient city on the east bank of the Nile in modern-day Sudan, famous in antiquity for its wealth and luxury.</note>,
And says: "This shall be to the health of that foreign beauty."
Now a cheer is heard from a thousand loud throats,
While the court music begins to delight the ear.

<margin>Flattery is the corruption of princes.</margin>
O wicked Flattery, hated enemy
Of true sincerity, who through a feigned love
Betrays majesty, and intends to attack the walls
Of the princely mind where it is weakest:
You honor the rising sun when it shines brightly;
But when a cloud obscures her, then you disappear
Like a shadow; yes, you shoot your evil arrows
When she sets, and can no longer light your way;
What mischief have you brought forth in the world!
How often have you violated heroic virtue,
When you know how to advise Princes toward wickedness?
What has innocent virtue not suffered through your evil deeds,
O wicked Deceiver? Had you not seduced **Adam**,
Perhaps humanity would still stand in its primal innocence.

<margin>They set out by night for the abduction;</margin>
The ignited passion rages ever more within.
The beautiful Sarah floats through the King's heart and senses:
And that unholy fire is steadily in his mind
Cherished and fed by courtly flattery.

It is clear that our History has not been recorded everywhere with equal detail by the Divine *Moses*, and while more is kept silent in one place, more is reported in another. The abduction <term>schaking</term> <note>Referring to the biblical account in Genesis 12 where Sarah is taken into Pharaoh's palace.</note> of *Sarah* to the Egyptian court—with which we begin our piece and which therefore required more extensive circumstances—provided us with these only sparingly; yet there are clear signs of where these events, though unmentioned, occurred more broadly. When King *Pharaoh*, after the abduction, gives *Abraham* gifts and treats him well for the sake of his sister *Sarah*, one clearly sees that an interval and postponement of the marriage occurred, and the reason why that forced union <term>echt</term> was not consummated remains unmentioned. Many researchers of Biblical antiquities have also observed this and guessed at the cause of this delay; one can find various conjectures about it in the works of the highly learned *W. Goeree* <note>Willem Goeree (1635–1711), a prominent Dutch bookseller and author known for his "Mosaize Historie" (1683), which mixed biblical history with secular archaeology.</note>, in his *Mosaic Histories*; yet all are without any certainty or proof. For this reason, I believe I may, with equal right, propose that the festival <term>hoogtyt</term> <note>A "high time" or major religious festival.</note> of *Isis*, celebrated so solemnly by the Egyptians, intervened—a time which forbade all joy until the Ox-god *Apis* <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, worshipped as a god; his "appearance" or discovery was a cause for great celebration.</note> revealed himself: nevertheless

He suggests that a religious festival for Isis and Apis might have been the reason the marriage was delayed, preventing the union before Sarah was returned.</summary>

And a disgrace to radiant honor! How often the features

Descend upon me, like a balmy summer rain,
And has added to me treasures, salvation, and prosperity.
God makes me rich, and I am satisfied with that wealth.

Therefore this remains far from me: I only wish to stipulate,

<margin>General joy in the Valley of Shaveh.</margin>
Now the joyful cheering rises to the very vaults of heaven.
The green meadow itself seems to leap and dance,
Proclaiming the freedom of the Siddimites <note>Siddimites: The inhabitants of the Valley of Siddim, who had been taken captive by the four northern kings.</note>,

The Commander Abram, and his wondrous skill in war.
Now happiness has filled the bowls to the brim,
Refreshing the hearts of the weary companions
With royal wine. Everyone is on their feet.
The crowds now swarm and mingle together,
Like ants on hot summer days.
The plunder is gathered, and one sees them lugging and carrying,
The dividing of the spoils, the treasures, and the cattle.
A noise is heard there, like the roaring of the sea
When the wind, exhausted from wrestling with the waves,
Falls into a slumber, and allows the sky to clear once more.

While the ground blossoms with flowers wherever they tread,

And Sarah follows them with wondering eyes;
And cries: O strange event! who ever saw the like?

<meta>catchword: ABRA-</meta>

Now my Abraham also grows great in the world’s eyes.
The wealthy Shepherd becomes a friend, an ally,
Of Abimelech, the Prince of the Philistines.
Now he gives cattle, and sheep, fruits, and wines,
<margin>And Abraham gives the King gifts</margin>
And all that agriculture yields through sweat and labor,
From his abundance, for the Majesty of Gerar
As a tribute; and he selects, besides these many gifts,
(As proof that he was the one who had the well dug)
Seven more ewes, with wool thick and soft,
The most fertile of the flock, and white as hail;
So that the King might receive them from his hand,
And the ownership of the well might never be in doubt;
They also gave to that place, so that it might always
<margin>After which ceremony the place is named.</margin>
Bear witness to their oath, the name of Beersheba <note>original: "Berſeba". The name means "Well of the Seven" or "Well of the Oath," referencing the seven ewes and the treaty made there.</note>.
When thus mistrust had vanished before friendship,
Abimelech departed with his commander-in-chief <term>Veltheer</term> Pichol:
And Abraham planted a grove, long after this time,
Dedicated to his prayers, in his solitude.

->### THE NINTH BOOK.<-

->Cc 2<-

<note>original: "Eert, zonder offerwet..." This passage describes a form of "Natural Religion," a popular concept in the 17th and 18th centuries suggesting that God can be known through reason and nature without formal church structures.</note>

He honors God without the law of sacrifice or the duties of a temple, guided by experience and the natural light of reason. The shade of the olive trees is his temple; there, in solitude, he lifts holy hands and speaks intimately with God in fervent prayer. This prayer, rising from the <term>altar of the heart</term> <note>The "heart-altar" (hartaltaar) signifies that true worship happens within the soul rather than a physical building.</note> like a deep sigh of pure reverence—as if carried on the air of a holy sacrifice—is a sweet incense to the eternal <term>Supreme Being</term> <note>Opperwezen: A common Enlightenment-era term for God, emphasizing His status as the highest entity in a rational universe.</note>.

The palm groves in the heart of the forest are the sanctuary where he celebrates his feasts and holy days. It is there that he slaughters his sinful flesh, his desires, and his evil passions, laying them as offerings upon the altar of virtue. Indeed, in humility, he surrenders himself entirely to the Divinity and to His love.

He knows nothing of priests or unholy sacrificers, nor of <term>scribes</term> <note>Schriftgeleerden: Traditionally referring to biblical scholars or lawyers; here used to suggest those who focus on the "letter" of the law rather than its spirit.</note> or arrogant orators. His spirit is untroubled by strife or church disputes, and his free intellect is never led astray by prejudice or by frivolous minds who are merely skilled in the appearance of truth. Instead, through <term>contemplation</term> <note>beſpiegeling: A meditative or philosophical reflection on divine truths.</note>, he sees the radiance and clarity of the Heavenly Majesty. In this state, he can behold the luster of God's attributes and perfect virtues through faith in the word of God’s grace—the promise of Paradise and the salvation promised to the world through His <insert>Seed</insert> <note>A reference to the "Seed of the Woman" from Genesis, traditionally interpreted in Christian theology as a prophecy of the coming Messiah.</note>. He finds endless inspiration to nourish his exalted spirit in the praise...

### ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.
<meta>catchword: It is</meta>

At that time, no weeds had yet sprouted from the earth, nor the deadly <term>aconite</term> <note>original: *akonyt*; a poisonous plant often used in classical and Renaissance poetry to symbolize the arrival of evil or the end of the Golden Age.</note>. of His perfect virtue; the sketch of holiness; the grace of eternal intellect, instilled in you; the divine resemblance of justice and truth: What a Lord you were! How were you, O Adam, not enraptured, moved beyond yourself, when you—from the hands of the infinite Almighty, with so many gifts of intellect, spirit, and strength—were brought in an instant into the <term>garden of delight</term> <note>original: *lusthove*; a poetic term for the Garden of Eden, emphasizing it as a place of pleasure and divine beauty.</note>, and saw the light, the life, and, from above and below, all the earth and heaven full of endless wonders!

The Holy Being in His Holiness.

# ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.
<meta>catchword: When</meta>

Just as my <term>Atoning Hero</term> <note>original: "Zoenhelt"; a poetic title for Christ common in 18th-century Dutch theology, emphasizing his role in the reconciliation between God and man.</note>, when all shall be accomplished,
Risen from the bonds of prison, from the grim grave,
Will be crowned with my honor and glory:
Then the stage of our plan shall be altered.
I shall provide a young ram, entangled by its horns
In thick bushes, and in prickly thorns,
Arranged for the altar, as a glorious <term>symbol</term> <note>original: "zinnebeelt"; an emblem or living image meant to convey a deeper spiritual truth.</note>
Of the holy sacrificial Lamb, intended and shared
With sinful humanity, to perish in his place
Upon these very hills, crowned with thorns;
Thus Isaac shall again become an example for my church.
Thus let our painting of the great work of grace shine
Through all the ages, before the eyes of posterity,
With broader perspective and a shifting of horizons.

<margin>The Savior promises to let Abraham see his day.</margin>
So spoke the Almighty, from his sapphire throne;
And the world's Prince of Peace, with a starry crown
Upon his head, and clothed in light full of glow and rays,
Raised his voice thus through the Halls of Supreme Peace,
Where He, in the midst of Mercy and Justice,

After that masterpiece of faith, and let him see my day,
Through all the times, and all that shall come to pass:
So that his high spirit may be seized with joy,
After such a heavy trial and long-extended desire."

And Sarah, only after it shall all be fulfilled.
But how much calamity does my soul not expect
From Sarah’s passion and the sorrowful aftermath?

Upon one of the mountains that I shall show you." <note>Abraham is quoting the divine command found in Genesis 22:2.</note>
This is that very mountain: here the sign stood firm.
See there the altar, here the fire, the knife, the bonds,
And here may God receive you as a sacrifice from my hands.

<margin>He who is ready to do the will of God;</margin>
"My Father," (spoke the Hero) <note>original: "de Helt" — Isaac is portrayed here as a "hero" of faith for his willing submission to God’s will.</note> "come then: I am ready
To do your will, in obedience to God.
Come then, my Father, let love not terrify you;
Feel free to spare your tears; in a few moments
I shall tread upon the stars, unburdened of this mortal part.
Come, bind my feet; come, bind both my hands fast,
Lest any idle terror cause the sacrifice to fail:
But no, let me first press you in both my arms."

<margin>Embraces his Father, and says farewell.</margin>

Say that I die willingly, at the divine command,
And pray that she also lets all her grief depart, for God’s sake.
Farewell, my Father; may God spare you in life!
I go, so young, before you to that perfect state,
And when you die, I shall, in snow-white raiment,
With Grandfather Terah, followed by the angelic throngs,
With palms in hand, welcome you there,
And lead you where God, amidst the joyful sound of salvation’s triumph,
Shall press the crown of piety upon your brow.
Farewell, farewell; may God give you other sons!
No young vine can cling more firmly to the elm tree," <note>original: "olmboom" — The "elm and the vine" is a classical metaphor for a devoted relationship where one relies on the other for support.</note>

<margin>And he contemplates the wanton court life.</margin>

And the court, where vanity built itself a temple;
Where one flatters the Great, <note>original: *Grooten*, referring to those in high social or political standing.</note> and learns artful feigning;

In winter sunshine, or cool summer shade,
Seated, where nature caresses their heart and senses;
And contentment in the soul breeds a delight,
Far nobler than the pleasure of the worldly Great,
Who in the glow of gold reject humility,
And, proud of their sham-happiness, constantly buzz where they are;
Like hornets in the warm sunshine,
Where they hover through the blossom-rich valleys!
Ah! how much unrest, how many dark cares wander
Through the whole city and the court, where everyone sweats and toils
For all that never satisfies an exalted soul;
For princely favor, and honor, and prestige, and power;
All snares for virtue, all tinsel <note>original: *klatergout*, literally "clattering gold," an idiom for fool's gold or something with a false, cheap glitter.</note> for the eyes!
Pale worry lives in soot-blackened cities,
And forges the chains of countless distractions,
The shackles that enslave man to vanity,
Or bury this short life in frivolities. <note>original: *dartelheên*, referring to playful but often reckless or superficial behavior.</note>

# ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.
<meta>catchword: Then</meta>

Just as my **Hero of Atonement** <term>Hero of Atonement: "Zoenhelt," a common baroque Dutch title for Christ, depicting the Savior as a champion who wins a legal and spiritual victory through his suffering.</term>, when all shall be accomplished,

I shall provide a young ram, entangled by its horns

To sinful humanity, so that on these very hills,
Crowned with thorns, He may perish in his place;

Through all the ages, before the eyes of posterity,
With broader insight and receding vistas of thought <note>original: "verschieten van gedachten." This uses the terminology of perspective in painting to describe how history allows people to see the "depth" and distant meaning of God's plan.</note>.

<margin>The Savior promises to let Abraham see His day.</margin>

Upon His head, and clothed in light full of glow and radiance,
Thus raised His voice through the high halls of peace,

Through all the ages, and what shall come to pass:
So that his high spirit may be seized with joy,
After such a heavy trial and prolonged longing.

Spare your tears freely; I shall in a few moments
Tread upon the stars, relieved of this mortal part.
Come, bind my feet; come, bind both my hands fast,

But no, let me first press you in both my arms.”

No young vine can cling more firmly to the elm tree,” <note>original: "Geen jonge rank kan om den olmboom vaster kleven". <meta>This page continues the poetic account of Abraham’s death. While the previous page described the physical passing and the soul's ascent to the gates of heaven, this page depicts his reception at the divine throne and the subsequent mourning of his family and the land of Canaan. The catchword "So" from the previous page connects directly to the opening line here.</meta>

### THE TWELFTH BOOK.
Nn 3
<meta>catchword: Yes</meta>

So Hero Abraham is led before the throne,
Where God’s Love embraces him, and the All-Sufficiency <note>The Dutch "Algenoegzaamheit" refers to God as 'El Shaddai,' the all-sufficient source of everything.</note>
Fills him; Wisdom enlightens him with knowledge;
Glory adorns him, and leads him up to higher steps;
Until there the Savior himself unlocks for him all the treasure
Of his grace; and pours out upon his brow
The horn of salvation, and says: an inheritance
So glorious and excellent is reckoned to you through my atoning death.
<margin>And the marriage of the Lamb.</margin>
Come now, Blessed of my Father, inherit the crown
Of victory! Come, my dearly beloved Son!
Sit at the table, with all my exalted Favorites.
Now he is, amid holy cheers and joyful singing,
Led to the marriage of the Lamb, in eternity,
Where the fullness of joy was prepared for him.

<margin>General sorrow for the death of Abraham.</margin>
But alas! how ghastly was the state of the fields!
How Hero Isaac mourns! Alas! how both his boys mourn! <note>Abraham’s grandsons, Jacob and Esau, who were fifteen years old at the time of his death.</note>
Into what a lament does Lady Keturah <note>Abraham's second wife after Sarah's death.</note> not burst,
As she now closes the eyes of her great Shepherd!
How Rebekah sighs, struck in the heart with grief!
How pitifully the house-steward is heard to complain! <note>Likely referring to Eliezer of Damascus, Abraham's long-time servant.</note>
And what a dismal cry sounds over the wide field!
All eyes weep for the death of the Hero.
All Gerar stands amazed; and Hebron begins to weep.
The hills sigh, and the hard rocks groan.
The flowing Jordan swells from the flood of tears.
The forest of Beersheba cries out toward Mamre;

<summary>This page describes Abraham's triumphant reception in heaven at the "Marriage of the Lamb" and contrasts it with the profound, universal mourning of his family and the landscape of Canaan.</summary>
<keywords>Abraham, Isaac, Keturah, Rebekah, Jacob and Esau, Hebron, Jordan River, Beersheba, Mamre, Marriage of the Lamb, mourning, Apotheosis</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the epic poem. While the previous page focused on Abraham’s soul being welcomed into heaven by the Savior, this page returns to the earthly realm to describe the public mourning across Canaan, the reunion of Isaac and Ishmael for their father's burial, and the author’s concluding reflections on his work.</meta>

# ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<margin>The rumor of which reaches Ishmael’s ears at the mountains of Paran,</margin>
Indeed, the entire land, as far as the City of Palms <note>original: "Palmstat"; a biblical name for Jericho.</note>, and much further,
Cries out as if with one voice: Alas, the great Shepherd,
Hero Abraham, the Prince of God, the land’s Ally,
The strong Tamer of tyranny <note>A reference to Abraham’s victory over the four kings in Genesis 14.</note>, is dead!
O disaster! O bitter woe! Do we also see Prophets fall!
So the mournful echo rolls around, and strikes the hills of Paran,
With sigh upon sigh, and with anxious woe! and ah!
Until it rings in Ishmael’s ears like a thunderclap,
Where he almost turned to stone from fright:

<margin>Who comes to mourn his Father, and with Isaac buries him in the cave of Machpelah.</margin>
He rouses himself in haste, and comes to where everyone was weeping,
And washes the cold bones of his Father with the moisture
That splashes from his crying eyes out of sorrow:
Until the precious corpse was magnificently, according to his worth,
Entrusted to rest in the earth in shady Machpelah:
There both sons, with tears on their faces,
Give an example of their virtuous duty <note>Despite their different paths, the Bible records that Isaac and Ishmael came together to bury their father (Genesis 25:9).</note>.

<margin>Conclusion of the history.</margin>
Now my task is completed; my poetic web <note>original: "dichtwebbe"; a metaphor comparing the composition of a long poem to the weaving of a tapestry.</note> is finished.
I have written twelve small books about Hero Abraham;
That great Man, followed from almost his cradle to his grave,
On all his journeys, from his first calling onwards,
Until where he triumphs in the highest arches of heaven,
Followed on the swift wings of the Poetic Arts:
And thus, in my verse, I have erected a monument <note>original: "eerzuil," literally an "honorary column."</note> to Religion,
Adorned with spiritual armor;
Upon which Holy Faith, after the end of my days,
Will perhaps continue to bear courage and glory for centuries to come.

<vocab>Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Machpelah, Paran, City of Palms, Patriarch, Poetic Arts, Holy Faith</vocab>

<summary>This final page describes the widespread mourning for Abraham throughout Canaan and his burial by his sons Isaac and Ishmael in the cave of Machpelah, ending with the author’s dedication of the twelve-book epic as a lasting monument to faith.</summary>

--- Page 433 ---
<meta>This page concludes the twelfth and final book of the epic. The previous page ended mid-sentence during the author's closing reflections, following the burial of Abraham by his sons Isaac and Ishmael.</meta>

# THE TWELFTH BOOK.

<margin>Comparison of this work with ancient epic poems.</margin>
The blind Greek <note>Homer, the legendary author of the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*.</note> sang of the heroes’ deeds of war;
The Mantuan <note>The Roman poet Virgil, born near Mantua, author of the *Aeneid*.</note> sang of Aeneas, the Trojan,
Who had fled burning Ilium <note>Troy.</note>, with his presumed gods,
And his Father, upon his shoulders:
I have sung of the great Abraham,
Who also took his Father out of Ur, the City of Fire <note>original: "Vuurstat"; a reference to the tradition that "Ur" means "fire" or "light" in Hebrew.</note>,
And, at God’s command, withdrew him from the paternal walls,
And the smoke of idolatrous altar-fires.
The Hero of Sulmo <note>The Roman poet Ovid, born in Sulmo, author of the *Metamorphoses*.</note>, whose Roman calendar
And festivals I imitated in my Dutch poetry <note>original: "duitsche poëzy"; in this period, "Duits" or "Nederduits" referred to the Dutch language.</note>,
Sang of his gods and their transformations:
All clever fables and learned trifles:
I sing of the Deity, who dwells in the unapproachable 
Light: my poem begins and ends with God,
And of His Truth, which I have painted from life
With genuine colors; I have given her as much ornament,
And, according to the capacity of my art, dressed her as richly,
As her majesty, of heavenly descent, allowed.

<margin>Conclusion of the work.</margin>
O God of Truth, who wished to light my humble verses
With the pure rays of Your Wisdom;
And often guided my spirit through Your Spirit:
To You be the praise, the thanks, all the honor and glory!
And if the world should ever wish to give me praise or honor;
It belongs to You: let it be ascribed to You alone!
For You, through Your power, breathed zeal into my soul, 
From the beginning to the very end of my work.

<meta>catchword: You</meta>

<summary>In this concluding passage, the author compares his epic poem about Abraham to the classical works of Homer, Virgil, and Ovid, asserting that his sacred subject is superior to pagan myths. The work ends with a humble prayer of thanksgiving, attributing the completion of the poem to divine inspiration.</summary>
<keywords>Homer, Virgil, Aeneas, Ovid, Abraham, Ur, Poetics, Divine Inspiration, Truth, Doxology</keywords>

--- Page 434 ---
<meta>This page concludes the twelfth book and the entire epic of Abraham the Patriarch. The author completes his closing prayer to God, transitioning from the previous page's unfinished praise of God's power to a final dedication of his literary labor.</meta>

# ABRAHAM, THE PATRIARCH.

...er,
You have lit the holy fire on the altar of my heart,
To burn this offering of my gifts to You:
Receive it favorably, and with a reconciled countenance.
Preserve my labor <note>The author refers to the completed poem as his "labor."</note> from the claws of Hatred <note>A common trope in early modern literature, where authors ask for protection against malicious critics.</note>,
And cherish my spirit, weary from wandering
Through fields of letters <note>original: "letterbeemden"; a poetic metaphor for the vast landscape of literature and study the author traveled through to complete his work.</note>, in the warm rays of the Sun of Salvation:
Indeed, let it, should death soon surprise me,
Still rest in the bosom of my Abraham <note>A dual reference to the biblical "Bosom of Abraham" (a place of peace in the afterlife) and the specific subject of his epic poem.</note>.

->T H E  E N D.<-

<summary>In this final passage, the author offers his completed work to God as a spiritual sacrifice and prays for his soul to find eternal rest. He concludes the epic by blending his literary achievement with a personal plea for divine favor and protection from criticism.</summary>
<keywords>prayer, sacrifice, heart-altar, literary labor, Sun of Salvation, Bosom of Abraham, conclusion</keywords>
